newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Central bankers give global economy good marks.
newsitem.headline: Central bankers give global economy good marks.

text.p: Central bankers from the world's leading industrial countries gave a generally upbeat assessment of the global economy on Monday but urged governments to press ahead with reforms if they want to spur more growth.

Central banks have already done their part by pushing down the price of borrowing money, so the onus is now on national governments to cut budget deficits and make job markets more flexible, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said.

Tietmeyer, chairman of the Group of 10 (G10) committee of central bank governors, told reporters after the committee's monthly meeting in Basle that many countries were seeing their economies start to gather momentum.
In Germany, Europe's economic powerhouse, gross domestic product in the second quarter rose 1.5 percent compared with the first three months of the year.

"It seems to be the case that there is a cyclical upturn," he said. "But one should not overestimate the second quarter figures because to some extent they are influenced by special seasonal factors in the first quarter," he added.
Tietmeyer said reports from the G10 governors showed that the global economy was also showing signs of strength. He specificially cited the United States, Canada and Japan.
The situation was mixed in Europe, he added, but he singled out Britain and the Netherlands as bright spots.
He urged governments in continental Europe to continue putting their budget deficits in order and to reform social welfare and labour laws to promote economic recovery.
"The (central banks') monetary policy is in an appropriate stance and can't do more for the time being," Tietmeyer said.

"Especially in continental European countries, it is important that the structural reforms are now continued and addressed even stronger...because fiscal policies and the adjustment process in social security systems are an absolute priority," he said.
"Besides that, an increase in labour flexibility is a necessity for lasting growth and for job creation."
Tietmeyer welcomed the dollar's recent strength, saying a strong U.S. currency benefitted everyone.

"We all agreed further dollar development is important and a strong dollar is in the interest of all," Tietmeyer said of the bankers' talks on exchange rates. "This is the common position of the G10," he added.
The G10 comprises the central banks of the United States, Canada, Japan, Germany, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden, Switzerland, Italy and Britain.
Tietmeyer also said central bank governors saw a good chance oil markets would remain clam for the next year.

"Concerning oil markets...there is a good chance for a quiet and stable development during the next 12 months," he said. "And of course this will have a positive effect not only on the world economy but also the region of the Middle East," he said.
